item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Phones have a habit of dying at the worst moments, and a regular power bank only helps if you remember to pack a cable. Magnetic power banks help resolve that problem by snapping onto the back of a compatible phone and wirelessly charging it while you keep using the phone. The Energizer Magnetic PowerBank is one of these types of chargers, and Best Buy has it on sale as part of a holiday deal for just $17.99.

The Energizer 10,000mAh Slim Metal Magnetic Wireless Power Bank (QM10081PQ) is a Qi2 and MagSafe-compatible power bank with a metal body 0.62 inches thick. It has a 10,000mAh lithium-polymer battery, up to 15W wireless output, a USB-C PD port, and a maximum total output of 20W.

$18 at Best Buy

Power that snaps onto your phone

Charge without the cables

This Energizer power bank supports Qi, Qi 2.0, and MagSafe, so it attaches magnetically to the back of a phone that supports those standards. Once it's on, you can keep scrolling, texting, or following directions without a cable dangling between the two. That's especially handy on a long commute or on a day of sightseeing when you're snapping pictures and taking videos (and as such draining the battery faster than normal).

With the PowerBank, you get a 10,000mAh battery, a practical size for long flights or being stuck at an office desk that's far from a wall socket. It's the kind of capacity you toss in a bag and forget about until you need it. The build is slim metal, and there's an LED display, which is a nice touch, especially for a charger under $20. You can wirelessly charge your phone with the Energizer PowerBank, and it also has a USB-C port for devices that don't support wireless charging.

8 tech tools every traveler needs on their next adventure

At $17.99, the Energizer Magnetic PowerBank is a solid pick if you want a cable-free way to keep your phone going. That's a $17 savings off its regular $34.99 price at Best Buy, and an easy way to add a backup battery to your travel kit.

item.title: I explored 4 terminals beyond Windows Terminal, and one was clearly ahead
item.itunes:title: I explored 4 terminals beyond Windows Terminal, and one was clearly ahead
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I recently wrote an article that discussed why Windows Terminal was still my home for PowerShell, WSL and SSH sessions, despite there being plenty of alternatives out there. It's one of the better default apps in Windows, but being good enough for a default is different than being the best option out there. I tried four different options beyond the one that came with the OS, and one rose above the rest pretty convincingly.

I tested dual-boot, WSL2, and VMs to run Linux apps on Windows, and only one was worth keeping

Dual-boot, VMs, and WSL2 walk into a Windows PC...

10
By  Ayush Pande

WezTerm is the one that completely changed the way I work

The first terminal I reach for now

WezTerm looks pretty unassuming on the surface, but it's incredibly capable under the hood. Its best feature is the fact that it's a multiplexer, which means splits, tabs, and any other kind of named workspace are built in and able to be used concurrently. Windows doesn't have a tmux equivalent, and this is the first terminal I've found that's able to properly replicate what it can do.

SSH functionality is there and also has a killer feature of its own: when you connect to a remote host and open new tabs, those tabs do not need to be authenticated individually again. This is something I run into all the time running a home lab, and it's one of the things that made this terminal a mainstay on my main workstation. Keeping a persistent SSH workspace between windows on Windows is worth trying WezTerm for alone.

Configuration happens all within one Lua file, which for some people will certainly be a pro, but I'm edging towards con. Writing some code to change a font isn't exactly my first choice, but the power of being able to carry my configuration file between Windows, macOS and Linux is a great feature.

Warp is the most ambitious of the bunch

Warp is far from your standard terminal. Most of the other terminals on this list stick pretty closely to what we think acts as a terminal, but instead of being a continuous scroll of text, Warp groups each command and its output into a block. These blocks can be copied, searched, shared, and manipulated as a unit. Its input line is a lot more like a code editor than a prompt, and it gets a lot of its feel from being attuned more towards being an "agentic development environment" where an AI agent can run commands and edit code for you. If that's your forte, then Warp is for you. It's not something I would personally replace my stock terminal client with though.

Microsoft have made a terminal that doesn't feel like it needs to be replaced

5
By  Ty Sherback

Tabby is a connection manager before it's a terminal

Though it can be used as both

Tabby is another cross-platform terminal option that's built on Electron, and its biggest strength by far is remote connections. The saving of SSH profiles and SFTP panel is an excellent feature for a home lab, but one of its more underrated features is serial support. If you manage network gear over a console cable or regularly flash microcontrollers, the serial support alone could justify installing it. The trade-off is the one that comes with every Electron app.

With just one tab open in Tabby, it was using over 300MB of my system memory. When you compare that to the ~40MB that both WezTerm and Windows Terminal use, it seems a bit ridiculous. This more or less disqualifies it for my use personally, but it doesn't make it a bad terminal. If you use a serial connection often and an SFTP panel is a must, I can see how you can look past its heaviness.

Tabby

22
By  Ayush Pande

Alacritty is the opposite of heavy

Fast and bare on purpose

If Tabby is heavier for the sake of more features, Alacritty is minimalist for the sake of being fast. It's stripped of pretty much everything that isn't used to make the window and text drawing quicker. It also has no tabs or splits built-in, which makes it bad for PowerShell use but it lacks those features because it expects you to use a multiplexer or window manager on your own. This works if you're working within WSL where tmux or Zellij fill those voids, but if you're doing anything else in a Windows environment, it's not worth it over the stock option.

By  Ayush Pande

Windows Terminal is pretty good on its own, too

The default option still has merit

Despite the fact that they have some great features, after trying each of these terminals, going back to the stock Windows Terminal didn't feel like the total downgrade I thought it would. Besides WezTerm, I'd still reach for it over the other alternatives because it nails the basics, though the third-party options are great for more specific use cases. It's installed by default, open-source, detects your shells automatically, supports profiles, works flawlessly with WSL, and is still being updated to this day.

item.title: It’s not just you: Steam is currently down for maintenance, and online capabilities are shot [Update]
item.itunes:title: It’s not just you: Steam is currently down for maintenance, and online capabilities are shot [Update]
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
UPDATE: 2026/11/17 18:35 EST BY SIMON BATT

It seems that Valve has gotten its services back online after its maintenance, as the Downdetector reports are in freefall and my own PC has gone back online. It appears all services have been restored, too.

Original article now follows.

Summary

  • Steam is down for maintenance: online features like downloads, Friends, cloud saves, and the store are offline.
  • Over 30,000 outage reports on Downdetector indicate widespread issues right now.
  • Not much to do, so all we can do is wait for Valve to restore services.

If you've tried to download your fave games off Steam or talk to your friends, there's a good chance you'll be hit with a "No Connection" error despite having a perfectly good connection. Well, it's not just you; people are reporting that Steam is down right now for maintenance, taking down all internet-based features with it.

Steam is down for maintenance, and a lot of services are affected

There's not a lot you can do

At the time of writing, just under 48,000 reports have come in on Downdetector claiming that Steam is down. Downdetector doesn't check for outages itself, and relies entirely on user reports. Valve usually runs maintenance on Steam's network around 3-6 PM Pacific Time, but this one has seemingly gone on for 30 minutes, and barely anything works.

I myself can verify that Steam is currently down right now. I cannot download any games, my Friends List is gone, my cloud saves are unfetchable, and my store page has been reduced to limited capabilities. Unfortunately, there's not a lot we can do right now, but at least you know that it's not just you.

item.title: I've used Plex for years without paying a dime, but somehow missed these free features
item.itunes:title: I've used Plex for years without paying a dime, but somehow missed these free features
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I got into media streaming pretty late, but ever since, Plex has been the only media server I've used. For all its faults, I've never felt that I was missing anything. Yes, it's not open-source, and many features are behind the Plex Pass, but my local streaming from a PC to a single TV has never needed those features. The free plan is more than enough for my needs, and after years as a Plex user, I only recently discovered everything it offers.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

From a breadth of live TV channels and custom media collections to music streaming and photo apps, the free Plex plan is actually better than most people give it credit for. Its features may not be unique, but combined with its slick UI and no-nonsense usage, it's still one of the best media servers out there, at least for local-only streaming.

Live TV channels

Plex had way more free stuff than I thought

It's impossible to miss the free shows and movies Plex keeps pushing, but the live TV aspect is what I completely missed out on during the first few years. It functions exactly like many other live TV setups on streaming servers like Jellyfin and Emby, as well as on streaming apps like Tubi, Roku, and more. However, its interface is what sets it apart, especially after the recent redesign.

I was surprised by the myriad options available in the live TV section when I was bored with my streaming watchlist. Vintage shows and iconic sports matches alongside live poker, movies, news, and cartoons kept me flipping through channels like it was the early 2000s. This feature doesn't enhance my local media streaming, but it offers an alternative when I don't want to doomscroll on YouTube or my own library without settling on anything.

OTA broadcasts with a tuner and antenna

Tune into free broadcast channels

Watching over-the-air (OTA) broadcasts may remind you of a time you fondly remember, but you can do it within your Plex app, too. Of course, you'll need to buy a TV tuner and antenna to do it, but it's worth mentioning for people who like to do a bit of everything on their TV. And what's better than doing it on the same app that has your local media, free on-demand movies and shows, and live TV channels?

Most people use a compatible USB TV tuner and an antenna for the respective broadcast standard in their region. Plex will show the broadcast channels in your region alongside its free, ad-supported streaming channels. Note that you won't get DVR recording or program guide functionality without the Plex Pass.

Creating custom collections

Make your large library easier to browse

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

Although many nice-to-have features are restricted to Plex Pass users, the free plan still lets you create custom collections, so searching your media library isn't a pain. Once your collection grows past a point, manually browsing your movies or TV shows can become ineffective. By grouping similar content into curated collections, you can easily find, say, movies from the same franchise or by the same director.

Plex's default categories and collections don't always cover everything; hence, custom collections fill the gap. You can even add filters to let Plex create smart collections on the fly, such as grouping recently released or unwatched media into different collections. This reduces the friction of selecting something to watch after you drop on your couch after a tiring day.

Plexamp for streaming your own music

Listen to your local collection in a new way

Music streaming apps like Spotify and YouTube Music are fine, but the Plexamp app (separate from the Plex app) offers a better way to enjoy your local music collection. The free plan is useful enough to consider it as a serious alternative for your local collection. YouTube Music lets me upload my own music, but those tracks aren't part of its recommendations. Plexamp offers this feature, plus advanced discovery and organization.

You also get visualizers and integrations with Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. And remote streaming of your music library remains free, too. The paid plan adds an equalizer, offline downloads, and sonic analysis to identify similar-sounding tracks from your library. That said, the free plan makes for a robust music streaming app on its own.

Plexamp
See at Google Play Store
I ditched music streaming in Android Auto for a local library, and it’s so much better

Android Auto plays my curated music library from my NAS, and Spotify can't compete with offline reliability

1
By  Dhruv Bhutani

Plex Photos for your local photo collection

The free tier may be enough for some people

Another separate app, Plex Photos, lets you stream your local photo collection from your PC or server to your iOS or Android smartphone. While you can create a photo library inside the main Plex app, the dedicated Plex Photos app offers a much better experience. Depending on the version of your main Plex app, you may not see photo libraries in it at all.

Plex Photos organizes your collection by timeline and uses a dynamic view and custom folder banners. Unlike the main app, which treats photos as standard media files, Plex Photos is built for an enhanced photo-viewing experience. The paid version unlocks automatic backup to your server, AI auto-tagging, and remote access.

Plex Photos
See at Google Play Store See at Apple App Store
I self-hosted my own Google Photos replacement, and it's better than what I was paying for

Immich-in my disappointment in Google.

By  Chandraveer Mathur

Plex Pass is overpriced, but you may not need it at all

If you're like me and only stream your movies, music, and photos on your local network, you probably don't need Plex Pass. I don't even use hardware transcoding, as all my movies and shows play directly on my Apple TV. Plex's free tier offers almost everything you need for local media streaming, and not just for movies and shows. With the Lifetime Plex Pass now priced at $750, not many people will be willing to jump.

item.title: I replaced ElevenLabs with a free open-source tool that runs entirely on my machine, without sending anything to the cloud
item.itunes:title: I replaced ElevenLabs with a free open-source tool that runs entirely on my machine, without sending anything to the cloud
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I already pay for enough AI subscriptions, so when a project widely described as the open-source ElevenLabs alternative passed 110,000 stars on GitHub, I wanted to know whether it could replace one. VoiceStudio promises voice cloning, video dubbing, and transcription that all run on your own machine, with no account. That's a big claim for a free app, even after Voicebox cloned a voice from a few seconds of audio, showing what local tools can do.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

So I installed it on my desktop, nestled inside WSL2, and paired it with AMD's Lemonade. I cloned my own voice and dubbed a German documentary clip into English. Then I took the PC offline and ran it again from a clean start. It worked, mostly, and the parts that didn't are worth knowing about before you try it.

My local LLM turns my voice notes into to-do items automatically, and nothing falls through the cracks

No more losing my half-formed ideas

1
By  Samarveer Singh

VoiceStudio and a local LLM both fit inside one WSL2 distro

The Windows installer is unsigned, so I went straight to Linux

My test machine is a Ryzen 7 9850X3D desktop with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090 and its 32GB of VRAM. VoiceStudio has a Windows installer, but the project's code-signing policy says Windows installers are unsigned while its signing application is pending, and I'd rather not argue with Windows about that. The Linux build supports CUDA, and WSL2 exposes the Nvidia GPU to Linux, so VoiceStudio 0.5.8 went into Ubuntu 24.04 LTS on WSL2 with one command.

My first attempt looked finished, but it wasn't. The setup was still pulling its Python environment, and nothing answered on the app's local port until it finished. Give it time, and don't assume it's ready just because you got your prompt back.

VoiceStudio handles speech on its own, but its smarter dubbing modes need an LLM to refine the translation. I installed Lemonade Server from its PPA on the same distro, added the CUDA backend, and pulled Qwen3.5-9B, a 6.4GB download at Q4. Having both services share one loopback address meant I didn't have to bridge anything between Windows and Linux.

The model needed one tweak. Asked to translate a German greeting, it used 281 tokens, nearly all of them thinking, to produce a five-word answer, which took about two seconds. Reloading it with reasoning switched off fixed that.

lemonade load Qwen3.5-9B-GGUF --llamacpp cuda --llamacpp-args "--reasoning-budget 0" --save-options

The same prompt then came back in 10 tokens and 87 milliseconds. That's already a win, and it adds up. Lemonade had logged more than a hundred requests by the time I'd translated a 15-line clip, including a handful of my own test prompts.

A settings page connects the two. Under Settings -> System -> LLM Providers, I picked the Custom provider, set the base URL to http://127.0.0.1:13305/api/v1, and typed in the model name. I also pasted the URL into the model field the first time and earned myself a 404, so check your clipboard before you blame the software.

I moved my local models from Ollama to llama.cpp, and the reason I stayed has nothing to do with speed

Convenience beats tokens generated per second, always

2
By  Abhinav Raj

Thirty seconds of Alice in Wonderland was enough to clone my voice

It copied my pacing, pitch, accent, and even my breathing

For a sample, I read the opening of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, which is public domain and felt appropriate for the rabbit hole I was heading down. I trimmed the recording to 30 seconds, imported it, and asked the clone to read something else. It was spooky.

It had my pacing, my pitch, and my accent, and it even reproduced my breath sounds. That last one is what sells it, because it stops sounding like a voice reading and starts sounding like a person talking. And I don't entirely like how easy that was.

It's quick, too. I used a small script that sends a 58-word paragraph to VoiceStudio's local API and times the result. The RTX 5090 produced about 20 seconds of my voice in 2.3 seconds, which is roughly 8.6 times faster than real time.

The clone isn't flawless on words I never recorded. In my first session, "mini PC" came out as "mini psss", and words ending in an "s" sound dragged on, the same way across three runs. One of the built-in voices got "PC" right but sounded metallic and obviously synthetic. On a later clean start, my clone got it right too, so the glitch isn't permanent. Regenerating didn't clear it for me, but a fresh start of the app did.

Dubbing took more hand-holding than I expected

For the dub, I used a 1-minute 45-second explainer about how the Alps formedfrom ZDF's Terra X series, which publishes clips under Creative Commons licenses; this one is CC BY 4.0. VoiceStudio transcribed it into 15 segments. Generating the English audio took about 15 seconds, with about 10GB of VRAM in use across the whole GPU, including the LLM.

My first dub sounded like a German speaker reading English, with stray consonant sounds before lines. On my next import, a popup I nearly missed said automatic voice cloning had been skipped because, it said, its speaker labels were only estimates based on gaps in the audio, and it pointed me to a diarization model. I made a voice profile from the narrator's own audio and assigned it by hand. The result was much clearer, though a faint hiss before some words remained.

item.title: Tasks in Gemini make Google's assistant handle all your chores for you
item.itunes:title: Tasks in Gemini make Google's assistant handle all your chores for you
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Gemini's new 'Tasks' will handle mundane errands so you can focus on bigger priorities.
  • It taps Maps, Wallet, Calendar, and your Personal Intelligence to find, call, and book services for you.
  • Gemini can place calls and book appointments, and will identify itself as an AI; Tasks is free in the US now.

It seems the world of AI tools has finally found its nudge. Companies have been pivoting their LLMs to help people get their daily tedious jobs done; we've seen a few models adopt new tools that let them go through your bank account details for insurance.

Now, Google has announced its new feature to accompany its brand-new Hydrogen model. It's called Tasks, and its main job is to help you get stuff done while you focus on more important matters.

Tasks in Gemini help you get more done

Why sweat the small stuff?

As announced in News from Google, the company has revealed its new tool for Gemini. Titled "Tasks," the idea is that you can hand Gemini a job you have to do while you do better things with your time. The real benefit is if you already use Google's services, such as Maps or Wallet, as Gemini can tap into them to make its decisions.

Here's an example Google gave for using this new tool:

"i pulled out Gemini and told it, "Our minivan is overdue for a service appointment. Please call the two nearest dealerships and figure out how to get an appointment early Friday morning over the next month or so."

"Because Gemini already knows we drive a 2019 Honda Odyssey and where we live through Personal Intelligence, it found the nearest shops on Google Maps and called both at once."

That last bit is especially interesting, as it means Gemini could essentially make phone calls in your stead and book things for you. Because Gemini had access to Google Calendar, it could find a suitable slot on Friday to schedule the service appointment.

But what did the people on the other end hear? Presumably, it's the same kind of voice you'd hear when using Gemini's live feature, but Google does claim that Gemini will identify itself as an AI assistant before doing anything, which is reassuring.

Tasks for Google is rolling out for free right now across the US.

item.title: This free app fixed everything that annoyed me about Windows 11's volume mixer
item.itunes:title: This free app fixed everything that annoyed me about Windows 11's volume mixer
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If there's one thing I don't like about Windows 11's audio controls, it's the way I have to access them. It gets on my nerves every time I want to adjust the volume of a particular app without affecting anything else. And that's despite Windows having a volume mixer that lets you do exactly that. The problem is that I need to click twice and scroll down before I can even get to the individual volume sliders. Sure, I could use the Windows + Ctrl + V keyboard shortcut to bring up the mixer, but that isn't all that convenient if I still have to scroll down.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

It doesn't help that I have multiple audio devices connected to my PC, either. Between my GoXLR, headset, and soundbar, the list of outputs that show up is longer than I'd like. That's what made me look for third-party options, and after a quick Google search and browsing through a couple of Reddit threads, I came across EarTrumpet. Now, I have a second volume icon sitting in my system tray, but I actually enjoy using this one.

These 3 free apps fix the Windows 11 quirks Microsoft still hasn't addressed

Windows 11 should've shipped with the features these apps offer

By  Hamlin Rozario

Same functionality, but much more convenient

EarTrumpet just puts everything in the right places

I don't get why Microsoft buries the volume mixer under a separate menu. I mean, if I'm clicking the volume icon in the system tray, I'd like to see all the sliders right away instead of having to look for them. That's exactly what EarTrumpet does, and I don't think it could've made things any simpler. Clicking its icon brings up a compact flyout with the master volume slider at the top and individual app sliders underneath. So if I want to quickly mute Discord, for example, all it takes is two clicks.

That's not all there is to it, though. You can expand the flyout to see all your playback devices and the apps using them. Considering I have a GoXLR set up, this takes up almost all the vertical space on my monitor because of all the virtual audio outputs it adds to Windows. But I actually prefer having all the sliders visible at once instead of having to select each playback device from a separate menu just to adjust its volume. It only took five minutes with EarTrumpet for me to start wishing Windows 11 made things this straightforward in the first place.

I don't even need the volume sliders half the time

Sometimes, all you have to do is scroll or press a key

As much as I like having all the volume sliders within reach, there are times when I don't even bother opening the mixer anymore. And that's thanks to EarTrumpet's mouse shortcuts. For starters, hovering over its icon in the system tray reveals the current volume level and the default playback device. While you're at it, you can simply use the scroll wheel to increase or decrease the volume. Or if you want to mute everything going through that device, you can just middle-click the icon.

These options are handy when I'm in the middle of a game and want to make a quick adjustment without opening another menu. If you prefer, you can even configure your own hotkeys to open the flyout, bring up the volume mixer, or increase/decrease the volume. Now, I'm not a fan of using keyboard shortcuts since it's hard for me to keep up with all the combinations I already use on Windows, let alone memorize a bunch of new ones just to control the volume. But it's always good to know the option is there just in case.

I still can't ditch the native volume icon, though

But it's not like I expected EarTrumpet to replace it anyway

The only thing that slightly annoys me about using EarTrumpet is that I now have two volume icons in my system tray. Even though I rarely click the wrong one, I'd love to get rid of the native icon and have EarTrumpet take its place. Except I can't because it's part of the Windows 11 Quick Settings panel, which I still use almost every day to toggle Wi-Fi, connect Bluetooth devices, and sometimes even enable Night light when I'm staying up late. So a cleaner system tray can't come at the cost of losing those controls.

But then again, I didn't install EarTrumpet thinking I'd no longer need the volume icon. I just wanted a more convenient way to access per-app volume controls, and this tool gave exactly that and more. Besides, EarTrumpet actually lets you switch to its legacy icon if having two identical volume icons bothers you so much. You can find the option in Settings -> General -> Legacy settings. I find that icon a bit tiny, though, so I'd rather stick with the default one.

Functionality is kind of pointless without ease of use

I think EarTrumpet is a great example of how much of a difference ease of use can make, even if it's nothing special in terms of functionality. Windows 11 already offers most of the same audio controls EarTrumpet does, but makes accessing them cumbersome. I get that there's no space in the Quick Settings panel, but why does the volume mixer have to be crammed into a tiny section in the bottom-right corner when there's so much vertical space to work with? All Microsoft needs to do is let users expand the Quick Settings panel to show all volume sliders at once. If and when that happens, I'll finally have a reason to ditch the second volume icon.

item.title: Your motherboard's CR2032 battery was never a standard, it just won by accident in the late 1990s
item.itunes:title: Your motherboard's CR2032 battery was never a standard, it just won by accident in the late 1990s
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Pretty much every desktop motherboard you can buy today has a CR2032 coin cell on it, and while that's been the case for long enough that it feels like a requirement, Intel's ATX specifications don't require it at all. Intel's own design notes for real-time clocks in chipsets recommend "Duracell 2032, 2025, or 2016," allowing manufacturers to use a thinner cell. All three of those cells are 3V and are 20mm across, differing only in thickness and capacity. According to Panasonic, the 3.2mm CR2032 has a capacity of 225mAh and the 1.6mm CR2016 has a capacity of 90mAh.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Way back in 1984, IBM put a battery-backed clock on its PC AT motherboard, and modern chipsets to this day are compatible with the Motorola chip that IBM used. That's not where the CR2032 started, though, as the AT shipped with a 6V lithium pack, and over the following decade, manufacturers used everything from external battery packs and rechargeable cells soldered to the board to sealed clock modules with batteries inside. It was only in the late 1990s that the CR2032 emerged as a default, but nobody required manufacturers to use it. Now, 30 years later, some are starting to do without a separate battery altogether.

The IBM PC AT shipped with a 6V battery

The clock came first

IBM's Technical Reference for the PC AT, dated March 1984, highlights the "Battery backup for CMOS configuration table and Real-Time Clock" as a feature of the system board. This is facilitated by a Motorola MC146818, which IBM describes as containing "the real-time clock and 64 bytes of CMOS RAM." The clock and its control registers took up 14 bytes, and the rest was used for the machine's configuration, including floppy types, hard drives installed, and how much memory it had.

Software accessed the chip through two I/O ports, writing an address to port 70h and then reading or writing data at port 71h. Those same ports are still used by modern PCs, and while CMOS is a manufacturing process, Intel recognizes that CMOS is "used interchangeably as the RTC's RAM."

The battery was plugged into a four-pin connector on the board, labelled J21, and IBM lists pin 4 as "6Vdc." IBM included a 6V lithium pack on a cable, and the system could detect if the battery failed through a status bit on the clock chip alongside a display 161 error on boot. IBM's suggested workaround in the Guide to Operations was a little grim, too. You could "continue to operate your IBM Personal Computer AT by running the 'Setup' program EACH time you turn your system unit's power on."

The 6V requirement came from the clock chip and how it was wired. Motorola's MC146818A datasheet rates it to run at a minimum voltage of 3V, but the AT's battery also went to the chip through a pair of isolation diodes. Across these, you could drop voltage, which would mean that a 3.6V battery could fall below the minimum operating voltage. If it does, while firmware settings would survive, the RTC could be left with intermittent updates, causing clock drift. Using a 6V pack gets around that issue by supplying plenty of headroom.

When it comes to the original IBM PC and the PC XT, there was no battery-backed clocks on either motherboard. Expansion cards were used to fill the gap, and AST's SixPakPlus, a memory and I/O card for the PC and XT, came with a "Clock-Calendar with battery backup." Its manual from June 1983 describes a "User-replaceable Lithium battery" held under a retaining clip, with a life expectancy of "approximately one year." In May 1984, AST published a technical bulletin listing compatible replacement batteries for its clock cards, including the Sanyo CR2032 and Varta CR2032. It may not have become the default just yet, but the CR2032 was already being used to keep time in PCs in the mid-1980s.

The RISC vs CISC debate is dead because both sides stole each other's best ideas

You may have heard that x86 is RISC on the inside, but what does that mean exactly?

2
By  Adam Conway

Clones used whatever battery they wanted

External packs, barrels, and sealed modules

IBM clones were common, and while they typically copied the AT's clock and its port layout, they didn't always copy the battery. In one example, Elitegroup's manual (published in 1988) for the ECS 386/32 says the board "does not have an onboard battery," instead requiring an external pack. Users could power it with four AA batteries or a purpose-built pack, and Elitegroup included a 3.6V lithium battery in the box. Asus took a similar approach with its ISA-386C in 1991, which also shipped with a separate 3.6V battery and accepted external supplies of up to 4.5V.

Manufacturers each approached it differently. Some, like one 486 board manual with a 1990 AMI BIOS, used an on-board rechageable battery or external battery, and Gemlight's boards from 1994 and early 1995 still offered either option. These external four-pin connectors were labelled "VDD (6V)." On-board cells were often nickel-cadmium "barrel" batteries, which are notorious among collectors for leaking. Michal Necasek of the OS/2 Museum described one 386 board as having "a dreaded rechargeable NiCd barrel battery near the keyboard connector," along with "hints of green copper oxide" where an earlier battery had leaked.

One other popular option was to put the battery inside the clock chip itself. Dallas Semiconductor's DS12887 was a "Drop-in replacement for IBM AT computer clock/calendar," with a lithium cell and a crystal sealed inside, with Dallas rating it for "over 10 years of operation in the absence of power." The downside, though, was that a flat battery usually meant replacing the entire module, and these chips lasted well into the Pentium era. Asus' April 1996 manual for the P/I-P55T2P4 even explains how to clear "the user-entered information stored in the Dallas DS12887A Chip."

Coin cells won when clocks moved into chipsets

And everyone eventually switched

In the early 90s, IBM had already begun using coin cells with some of its own motherboards. A technical guide for its PS/2 Model 90 XP 486 and Model 95 XP 486 published in October 1990 describes "a flat 3-V coin cell" with a life expectancy of "7 to 10 years depending on system usage." By August 1994, IBM's consumer-focused Aptiva came with a Hardware Handbook specifically instructing owners to "Replace the battery with a 3-volt (CR2032) lithium battery only," on a board that still took a 486 processor. Other manufacturers continued using external packs and sealed clock modules, though, and the reason for that was partially where the clock itself was located.

When the clock was a separate chip, companies often used a Dallas module, but once chipset makers integrated the clock into their own silicon, motherboard manufacturers were able to supply backup power directly instead. One datasheet from SiS for its 85C497, part of a 486 chipset from July 1995, described an internal real-time clock with a "Battery Power Input" and a current draw of just 2.02µA at 3V. VIA's VT82C406MV companion chip from April 1995 also integrated a Dallas-style clock, while the VT82C586A from October 1996 has a pin called VBAT, described simply as "Battery input for internal RTC."

In terms of power consumption, coin cells were the most practical choice, as a clock drawing around 2µA can run for years on a CR2032. Intel later integrated the RTC into its PIIX4 southbridge in April 1997, describing A Motorola "MC146818A-compatible real-time clock with 256 bytes of battery-backed RAM" powered by "a separate 3V lithium battery that provides up to 7 years of protection." The same datasheet says its RTC power plane is "Typically, powered via 'coin-cell' lithium battery."

Asus' own boards mark the transition from 1996, too. The P/I-P55T2P4 from April uses Intel's PIIX3, which relied on an external clock chip, and packs a Dallas module. The P/I-P55SP4V from December uses SiS's 5596 chipset instead, and its motherboard diagram shows a round holder labelled "CR2032 3Volt Button Cell Battery." Asus's later Intel boards are similar, with the PIIX4-based TX97 from August 1997 and P2B from December 1998 both showing a "CR2032 3V Lithium Cell" too.

ATX wasn't the cause of this; the TX97 is a Baby AT board, and none of the ATX specifications I could find actually name a specific battery. In fact, in 2001, Que's A+ Certification study guide by Mark Soper and Scott Mueller said that "The CR2032 battery has become the most common removable battery on Pentium-class systems," while still listing the Dallas DS12887A as another type you could come across. ATX didn't have a requirement to use a CR2032, and it had simply emerged as the preferred choice for integrated RTCs, making it so manufacturers adopted replaceable 3V coin cells.

Your CPU still boots up pretending to be a 1978 Intel chip, and Intel gave up on removing it

Both Intel and AMD CPUs pretend to be an Intel 8086 when they boot up, and Intel gave up on getting rid of it.

7
By  Adam Conway

Modern PCs still use the PC AT's clock interface

It never went away

Looking to more modern chipsets, like Intel's 800 series, its datasheet says the chipset "contains a real-time clock functionally compatible with the Motorola MC146818B," with "256 bytes of battery-backed RAM." It still uses ports 70h and 71h, and runs on "a 3 V battery or system battery if configured by design as the source." AMD has maintained similar compatibility, with its 2016 developer guide for Family 16h processors describing a bit in register D indicating that the "RTC date, time, and CMOS RAM are invalid due to low RTC battery." This is the same bit and the same register used by the IBM PC AT to detect dead batteries in 1984.

On a desktop, the battery isn't responsible for a whole lot. Intel notes that the chipset clock calculates a minimum battery life of 3.88 years under a number of assumptions, while also saying that standby power "will significantly increase the RTC battery life." As well, the coin cell battery is only used when there isn't another power source, meaning that this timespan is likely far longer for most desktop PCs. If power is lost, the battery can keep the clock running and a small block of CMOS memory alive, though most BIOS settings on a modern motherboard are stored in non-volatile flash memory and don't depend on it.

Your operating system may not rely on the time kept by the motherboard these days, either. On Linux, for example, its RTC driver will write back to the CMOS clock every 11 minutes when there's an external time source. As for Windows, it has its own longstanding conventions for the hardware clock. Microsoft's Raymond Chen explained in 2004 that Windows traditionally kept it on local time rather than UTC because people dual-booted with "MS-DOS and Windows 3.1," which "operate on local time."

Some manufacturers are starting to drop it

Not every computer needs a separate RTC battery

Microsoft has, for just over a decade, been accounting for devices without a dedicated RTC battery. In November 2015, Windows 10 added Secure Time Seeding, which estimates the current time using information gathered from network connections. Microsoft says that "PCs and big form-factor hardware have a dedicated battery to power their system clock," while pointing out that smaller devices often don't. Secure Time Seeding isn't perfect, though, and in the past, it was the cause of the clock on some servers drifting weeks or even years from the correct time.

Framework has gone even further, dropping the separate RTC battery from its 13th Gen Intel and Ryzen 7040 laptops and using the main laptop battery to keep the clock running instead. Framework's reasoning for this is that it reduces the environmental impact and helps it comply with safety requirements for coin cells. If the main battery and external power are both disconnected, the clock resets, but the operating system can restore the correct time when it next connects to a network time server.

Dell, meanwhile, is taking a different approach with its PowerEdge servers. Starting with firmware updates for its 14th-generation systems in August 2024, Dell has changed how servers respond to a failed or removed coin cell. BIOS settings were already stored in non-volatile memory, but removing the battery, according to Dell, would reset them "for consistency with prior behaviors and user expectations." Updated firmware preserves those settings, and Dell says that for most users, the impact of replacing the battery "is not worthwhile."

On desktop, it doesn't seem like things are changing anytime soon. Desktops don't have main batteries to fall back on, and all major motherboards still use a CR2032. You could use other 3V coin cells to power the same type of clock, but they're not always interchangeable. For example, a CR2016 has the same diameter and voltage as a CR2032, but it's half as thick, so a holder built for a CR2032 may not enable a smaller battery to make proper contact.

The CR2032 has made its way to most modern PCs, yet there was never a specification requiring it, and it's taken 30 years for companies to realize that they may not need it anymore. For now, though, the CR2032 is still the default on desktop motherboards, even if it was never a requirement.

All three of those cells are 3V and are 20mm across, differing only in thickness and capacity. According to Panasonic, the 3.2mm CR2032 has a capacity of 225mAh and the 1.6mm CR2016 has a capacity of 90mAh.

The clock came first

IBM's Technical Reference for the PC AT, dated March 1984, highlights the "Battery backup for CMOS configuration table and Real-Time Clock" as a feature of the system board. This is facilitated by a Motorola MC146818, which IBM describes as containing "the real-time clock and 64 bytes of CMOS RAM." The clock and its control registers took up 14 bytes, and the rest was used for the machine's configuration, including floppy types, hard drives installed, and how much memory it had.

Software accessed the chip through two I/O ports, writing an address to port 70h and then reading or writing data at port 71h. Those same ports are still used by modern PCs, and while CMOS is a manufacturing process, Intel recognizes that CMOS is "used interchangeably as the RTC's RAM."

The battery was plugged into a four-pin connector on the board, labelled J21, and IBM lists pin 4 as "6Vdc." Clones used whatever battery they wanted

External packs, barrels, and sealed modules

IBM clones were common, and while they typically copied the AT's clock and its port layout, they didn't always copy the battery. One other popular option was to put the battery inside the clock chip itself. item.title: Apple is experiencing a widespread outage, with iCloud and several other services down
item.itunes:title: Apple is experiencing a widespread outage, with iCloud and several other services down
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Multiple Apple services, including iCloud, App Store, and Apple Pay, are experiencing outages.
  • Apple says an internal update caused the disruption; many systems are back online, but some iCloud sign-in errors persist.
  • The outage follows recent major service failures from Microsoft, FAA disruptions, and an NSA internal network incident.

Several Apple services, including iCloud, the App Store, and Apple Pay, are down right now. According to Downdetector, reports started earlier today, but the outage is still ongoing as of 4pm ET.

Apple's Status Page lists iCloud, iCloud Web Apps, Apple Business, Apple School Manager, and more as experiencing issues, while it says problems with AppleCare on Device, the App Store, and more have been resolved. Despite Apple's Status Page indicating several services are back online, reports of users experiencing problems can still be found on social media platforms.

For what it's worth, iCloud seems to be working fine for me right now. In a statement to multiple publications, Apple said the following regarding the ongoing outage:

"Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible."

Some users are still experiencing issues with iCloud and related Apple services

Apple's issues follow Microsoft's services outage last week

Some users have reported being signed out of iCloud on iPhone and Mac, followed by verification failures and sign-in errors. Apple's service issues follow Microsoft's apps and tools outage last week, which left millions of users unable to access email through Outlook, Teams, and various Microsoft 365 products.

Following the Microsoft outage, all US flights were grounded for hours after a major Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) systems failure, delaying and canceling thousands of flights. Then earlier today, CNN reported that the National Security Agency (NSA)'s internal NSANet network went down. The NSA later confirmed the report, but said that "mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues."

The US government's highly classified national security communications network is reportedly experiencing a major outage

CNN says it has spoken to several sources at the NSA

By  Patrick O'Rourke
